description: Just a team to participate and have fun.
summary:
Flashpoint maps 1,276 NASA microgravity fire tests by oxygen and pressure, next to the ISS, Moon Base and spacesuit atmospheres. For any atmosphere, it counts the nearby tests by fuel type, shows how those fires ended, and ranks NASA’s 24 combustion investigations. An SI assistant answers questions from that evidence only, and every number is checked before it appears. It is also able to point the user to different location on the website.

This answers the challenge by turning PSI’s scattered records into fire safety insights a designer can use, and by extracting data ready for predictive modeling. It matters because the map shows where the evidence runs out. Those gaps show which experiments are needed before people live on the Moon.

A learner page is also available, teaching early learners using interactive experiments,  animated lessons with narration (AI-Assisted), and a formula sheet including everything taught prior.
details:
Flashpoint shows what NASA’s microgravity fire tests say about the air astronauts will breathe. Choosing a cabin atmosphere is a trade-off: lower pressure makes spacewalks easier, but the crew then needs more oxygen, and more oxygen makes materials burn more readily.

We placed 1,276 tests from NASA’s Physical Science Informatics database on a map of oxygen against pressure, next to the planned habitats. Pick any atmosphere and the site shows how many tests sit nearby for each fuel type, how those fires ended, which of NASA’s 24 combustion investigations tested closest to it, and a printable evidence brief. An SI assistant answers questions from the same evidence, cites its tests, and has every number checked before it is shown, with a rule-based fallback.

The map also shows where the evidence runs out. ISS air has 312 nearby tests, Moon Base air has 68, all fuel droplets, and spacesuit air has none. None of the 263 solid-material tests can be placed, because NASA’s tables give them no pressure. Those gaps mark the experiments needed before people live on the Moon.

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript (SVG map, WebGL flame lab), Python and TypeScript for the data, Google Gemini through a Vercel function, Playwright for testing and ElevenLabs for the AI-labelled narration. The team directed AI coding assistants and reviewed every change.

For prediction we count nearby outcomes instead of fitting a model. NASA’s outcome labels differ between experiments and airflow was recorded for only 13 tests, so a fitted model would mostly learn which experiment a test came from.

We invented no data, linked every number to its NASA record, labelled illustrations and AI answers, and the site never calls an atmosphere safe. It works on phones, in light and dark themes, and from the keyboard.
